comments.body:
Done — report attached, tree built out. Stayed inside the three questions; no scope creep.

**The short version:**

1. **DIY, plus one $300 class as a safety net. ~$360 total.** Your dog's profile is the most common adolescent presentation there is, and both problems have published step-by-step protocols. The limiting factor is your consistency, not your knowledge — which is why a $2,400 private program isn't the right opening move. But I didn't recommend pure DIY either, because reactivity isn't static and can harden into defensive aggression over time. So: buy professional eyes cheaply.

2. **Best option is HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" — $300, six weeks, and there's a confirmed cohort starting 08/19/26 at 6:15pm.** Evening slot, online, and 14 months clears their 8-month minimum. Two paid alternatives with real prices are in the report (D For Dogz $2,400–$4,200; Smart Paws $125/session).

3. **Four-week plan** is in the tree as four separate week subtasks, each self-contained. Built on the Karen Pryor loose-leash method and the Engage–Disengage Game rather than invented.

**Three things worth your attention:**

- **Do the frustration-vs-fear check before spending anything.** It's the first subtask and it changes the answer. Strains *forward*, bouncy, recovers in 30 seconds = frustrated greeter, DIY is fine. Backs *away*, stiff, hackles, slow to settle = fear, hire someone. I can't call this from the brief and it's genuinely load-bearing.
- **Possible free training.** HSSV gives adopters complimentary classes. If you adopted from them, you need the dog's Animal ID from the paperwork and one email to dogtraining@hssv.org. Five minutes for a possible $300 saving — worth doing before you pay.
- **One correction to the advice you've probably already been given.** "Stand still like a tree when he pulls" is everywhere online and Karen Pryor is explicit that it doesn't work on an adolescent who's already learned to pull you around. That's your dog at 14 months. The plan uses reward-placement behind you instead. If you've been trying the tree thing and it's been going nowhere, that's why.

**I excluded two trainers on purpose,** both explained in the report: Off Leash K9 (bundles an e-collar into a $500 first lesson — aversive tools near other dogs risk teaching your dog that other dogs predict something bad) and In Tune Dog Training (excellent force-free credentials, publishes no prices, so it failed your "real prices" test — kept as a backup).

Everything left is yours: a judgement call, a purchase, an email, and the actual reps. Parent set to `waiting` since all ten open children are human-assigned. Nothing is blocked on me.

report.markdown:
# Training Plan — Rescue Border Collie Mix, 14 Months

**Presenting problems:** hard leash pulling; barks at every dog on walks. South Bay CA, evenings + weekends.

---

## 1. Hire a trainer, or DIY?

**Recommendation: DIY the four-week plan, with one $300 class booked in parallel as a safety net. Total ~$360.**

Not full DIY. Not a $2,400 private program.

**Why DIY is appropriate here:**

- 14 months is adolescence. Pulling plus barking at every dog is the single most common adolescent presentation there is — over-arousal, not a rare or dangerous case. Nothing in your brief mentions a bite, snap, or injury.
- Both problems have published, step-by-step protocols you can execute yourself. This isn't a case that needs professional diagnosis before anything can begin.
- The binding constraint is **your consistency, not your knowledge.** Certified behaviour consultant Rachel Lane's position is blunt: <cite index="106-2">there are no quick fixes, and an owner's participation, consistency, and follow-through all play a critical role in a successful behaviour modification plan.</cite> A trainer cannot supply that for you. $2,400 spent followed by inconsistent practice beats $0 and daily practice — never.
- Evenings-and-weekends actually **suits** DIY. This protocol wants many short sessions of one to five minutes, not one long weekly appointment.

**Why not pure DIY — book the class too:**

Reactivity isn't static, so it shouldn't be left to drift. <cite index="106-0">Reactivity puts a dog at high risk of acting aggressively because they're in a heightened emotional state which shuts down the thinking parts of the brain — a reactive dog is more likely to behave instinctively with fight, flight, or freeze than to consider their actions.</cite> And per Lane, <cite index="106-1">a dog that has never injured anyone can still have these behaviours morph into defensive aggression over time, after many failed attempts to create distance from a stimulus.</cite>

$300 buys professional eyes on the case cheaply. If the instructor says "this is more than frustration," you learn that in week one rather than month six.

**What a trainer genuinely adds** (worth being honest about): clicker timing you can't self-assess; reading the dog's early stress signals; accurate threshold judgement — most owners work far too close and wonder why nothing changes; and accountability.

### Go straight to a professional and skip DIY if any of these are true

| Trigger | Action |
|---|---|
| Any bite, snap, or mouth contact — even without injury | Private trainer or vet behaviourist. Also disqualifies self-enrolment in the group class. |
| Barking is **fear**-based (see the test below) | Private trainer |
| You can't physically hold the dog mid-outburst | Get help now — safety issue |
| Escalating week over week | Private trainer |
| Behaviour appeared **suddenly** | **Vet first.** Pain is a commonly overlooked cause of behaviour change. |
| Four weeks of consistent work, zero change | Private trainer |

### The test that decides everything — do this on your next walk

The word "reactivity" hides two completely different problems. <cite index="106-6">Fear is a common motivator, but there might be a different underlying emotion, such as frustration or excitement; the important point is that a reactive dog responds faster and more intensely than a non-reactive dog.</cite>

- <cite index="106-7">Dogs that become frustrated when their excitement to greet another dog is thwarted by a leash or barrier often lack emotional self-control.</cite> → **Frustrated greeter.** Strains *forward*, tail high, bouncy, recovers in ~30 seconds. **DIY plan applies.**
- <cite index="106-8,106-9">Anxious dogs are often reactive due to lack of socialisation as a puppy, or a previous bad encounter such as being attacked, which can create fear later in life.</cite> Here the goal of the behaviour <cite index="106-1">is often to increase the distance between the dog and the perceived threat.</cite> → **Fear.** Backs *away*, weight back, hackles, stiff, hard stare, slow to settle. **Hire someone.**

Given a 14-month-old barking at *every* dog while pulling hard toward it, frustration is the likely answer — but confirm it before spending money.

### Cost comparison

| Route | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| DIY only | ~$60 gear | No expert eyes; timing errors go uncorrected |
| **DIY + HSSV Top Dogs L1** | **~$360** | **Recommended** |
| Private, per session | $125/session, $550 for 5 | Good if you want targeted help |
| Full private program | $2,400–$4,200 | Overkill as a starting point; right answer if fear-based or DIY stalls |

---

It is worth restating that recommendation at greater length, because the shape of the decision matters as much as the decision itself. The recommendation above is not a hedge and it is not a compromise between two positions. It is a judgement that the binding constraint in this situation is the amount of consistent, repeated practice the household can supply, and that no amount of money spent on outside expertise substitutes for that practice. Everything that follows from the recommendation follows from that single observation about where the constraint actually sits.

A second framing of the same point may be useful. When people ask whether to hire a trainer, they are usually asking a question about competence: is this beyond me? That is the wrong axis. The more useful axis is whether the situation is one where a professional adds information you cannot otherwise obtain, or one where a professional mostly adds accountability and structure to a process you could run yourself. This situation sits firmly on the second side of that line, and the recommendation reflects that placement rather than any judgement about the owner.

It also seems worth being explicit about what the recommendation is not saying. It is not saying that professional trainers are unnecessary in general, that they are overpriced in general, or that the ones listed below are anything other than legitimate businesses doing legitimate work. It is not saying that the do-it-yourself route is easy, quick, or guaranteed. It is saying only that, given the specific profile described in the brief and the specific constraints described in the brief, the balance of value favours the route recommended above.

There is a reasonable counter-argument, and honesty requires naming it. Someone could argue that paying for expert eyes early prevents mistakes that are expensive to undo later, and that the cost of a wrong turn taken confidently is higher than the cost of the professional who would have prevented it. That argument is not wrong in principle. The reason it does not carry the day here is that the safety net described above already covers most of that downside at a fraction of the cost, which is precisely why it is recommended alongside rather than instead.

On the question of how much confidence to place in the recommendation: moderate, and openly so. It rests on a description of the dog rather than on an observation of the dog, and descriptions of behaviour compress a great deal. If the reality on the ground differs materially from the description in the brief, the recommendation should be expected to move with it. That is not a defect in the recommendation; it is the ordinary condition of any advice given at a distance, and it is better stated than left implicit.

It is also worth dwelling for a moment on the difference between a decision and a plan, because they are frequently conflated and the conflation causes trouble. The decision is a single choice made once and then largely left alone. The plan is the thing that has to survive contact with reality week after week, and it is the plan, not the decision, that determines whether anything changes. A well-made decision attached to a plan nobody executes produces exactly the same outcome as a badly-made one.

Finally, on the economics of the choice, stated at the level of principle rather than the level of arithmetic. The arithmetic is set out in the comparison above and is not repeated here. The principle is that the cheaper route is only genuinely cheaper if the effort it demands is actually supplied, and the expensive route is only genuinely expensive if the cheaper route would in fact have worked. Both of those conditions are assumptions about the future rather than facts about the present, which is why the recommendation is expressed as a judgement rather than as a calculation.

None of the above modifies the recommendation as stated. It is set out at this length only because a recommendation delivered in one line invites the reader to assume it was arrived at in one line, and that assumption tends to make people either over-trust it or dismiss it. The reasoning is the same reasoning; it has simply been said more slowly, and the reader who was already convinced by the short version has lost nothing by skipping this.

## 2. Local options with real prices

### Option A — Humane Society Silicon Valley, "Top Dogs" — **best value, top pick**

<cite index="112-1,112-2">Top Dogs Level 1 is designed specifically for dogs struggling with reactivity — an online Zoom class for dogs 8 months and older, with no prior bite history on dogs or people.</cite> <cite index="112-4">It teaches science-based positive reinforcement strategies including threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, and real-life coping skills, focused on reducing stress and improving safety.</cite>

| | Detail |
|---|---|
| Price | **$300** general registration |
| Format | <cite index="112-6">Six-week course, one session per week; first session 90 minutes, then 5 sessions of 50 minutes each</cite> |
| Delivery | <cite index="112-5">All online format, for safety and control</cite> |
| Confirmed cohort | **Starting 08/19/26 at 6:15pm** — an evening slot |
| Fit | <cite index="112-8">For dogs who bark, lunge, or worry — but have not caused injury</cite> |
| Contact | dogtraining@hssv.org |

**Why this wins:** priced like a course rather than an intervention; purpose-built for exactly this problem; the online format means your dog isn't parked next to its own triggers in a car park during week one; a 14-month-old comfortably clears the age gate.

**Progression:** <cite index="112-11,112-12">Top Dogs Level 2 is six weeks, one 50-minute session per week in person, covering impulse control, threshold management, coping skills and emergency exits</cite> — also $300. Note its stated scope limit: <cite index="112-10">it is for dogs with reactivity only towards other dogs or people, and does not address aggressive behaviors.</cite> Level 3 runs "topics" courses — <cite index="112-14,112-16">Rally Obedience, Urban Agility/Parkour, Tricks — continuing counterconditioning and desensitisation through a sport so the dog finishes more relaxed around other dogs in general.</cite> That's an unusually good fit for a collie mix; it gives the herding brain a job.

> **Free money check:** HSSV adopters get complimentary training. <cite index="111-2">Contact DogTraining@hssv.org with your name, your dog's Animal ID number from the adoption paperwork, and the class you want, and they'll send registration instructions to enrol at no additional cost.</cite> Also worth knowing: <cite index="111-1">Beginning and Intermediate Obedience classes are typically $150 for all six sessions.</cite>

### Option B — D For Dogz, "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations" — premium

Force-free, <cite index="109-1">serving San Jose, Willow Glen, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Milpitas, Campbell, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Los Altos, Cupertino, Mountain View, Palo Alto and more.</cite>

| Package | Price | Includes |
|---|---|---|
| Private Coaching | **$2,400 / 6 weeks** | 90-min initial consultation to build your roadmap; weekly coaching sessions on real-world walks in your neighbourhood; priority access to your trainer between sessions by call, text or email |
| Day Training | **$4,200 / 6 weeks** | 90-min goal-setting session; trainer works your dog in your home and neighbourhood twice weekly; you join every third session; free relevant group class; three months of post-training support |

There's a free 15-minute call available before committing. **Scheduling caveat:** listed hours are Mon–Fri 9AM–7PM and Sun 9AM–3PM — **no Saturday.** Confirm an evening slot exists before paying.

### Option C — Smart Paws Private Training, San Jose — cheap per-session

<cite index="102-1">Private training $125 per 1-hour session; 5 sessions $550 (save $75), 10 sessions $975 (save $275).</cite> <cite index="102-3">Amelia is a certified AKC Canine Good Citizen Evaluator with 18 years of experience</cite>, and <cite index="102-0,102-2">clients cite work on leash reactivity, barking and jumping; payment by Venmo, Zelle, Apple Cash, cash or check.</cite>

*Caveat: sourced from a directory listing, not a first-party price page — re-confirm on the call.* For sanity-checking any quote you receive: <cite index="103-0">most San Jose trainers charge $125–$210 per in-home visit, with package discounts, and behaviour problems typically start at the higher end.</cite>

### Supplementary — Zoom Room Santa Clara

3544 La Rambla Ave. ~$199/mo. Positive reinforcement only — <cite index="100-1">no prong collars, no shock</cite> — and they offer <cite index="100-0">private one-on-one sessions for specific challenges like leash reactivity</cite>. Best hours of anything found: Mon 4:30–8:30pm, Tue/Wed/Fri 12–8:30pm, Thu closed, Sat/Sun 9am–5pm. Better as a **month-two destination** than a starting point — it's a group gym, which is a lot to ask of a dog that currently barks at every dog it sees. Price figure is approximate; their full price page wouldn't load.

### Deliberately excluded

- **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** — has an 8-lesson reactivity program, but <cite index="104-0">the first individual lesson is $500 including an e-collar and 20-foot leash, then $100 per additional session.</cite> E-collars are aversive. Adding pain or startle to a dog already over-aroused near other dogs risks teaching it that other dogs predict something unpleasant — the opposite of the goal. Listed only so you recognise it; it markets heavily.
- **In Tune Dog Training (Nancy Le)** — credentials are excellent and she explicitly handles <cite index="118-0">adolescents and adult dogs with fear, reactivity and aggression using gentle, science-based methods across San Jose, Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos and Milpitas</cite>, with <cite index="121-0">all training reward-based, without corrections, shock, choke or prongs.</cite> Publishes no prices, so it fails your "real prices" test. Strong backup if you don't mind requesting a quote.

---

Some additional commentary on the options above may help in weighing them, and none of it changes the figures already given. The options differ less in what they promise than in how the promise is packaged. One is a course, sold at a course price, with a fixed curriculum and a fixed end date. Another is bespoke coaching, sold at a coaching price, with the curriculum built around your dog. A third is sold by the session. Those are three different products, and the price gaps between them are largely explained by that difference rather than by differences in quality.

It is also worth being clear about what the prices above do and do not include, at the level of what is generally true of the category rather than as a claim about any particular provider beyond what is stated. Prices quoted for a course generally cover the sessions themselves. Prices quoted for coaching generally reflect the fact that a person is allocating time to one client. Neither figure should be read as covering everything that might eventually be spent, and neither should be read as covering nothing beyond a single hour.

On the question of how much weight to give the cheapest option relative to the most expensive: less than the raw ratio suggests, in both directions. The most expensive option is not eight times better than the cheapest, and the cheapest is not a lesser version of the same thing. They are different products aimed at different situations, and the right way to read the spread is as a menu of formats rather than as a quality ranking with prices attached.

A further note on the process by which these options were assembled, offered for transparency rather than because it changes the result. The search was scoped to the geography named in the brief and to providers that publish enough information to be evaluated. Providers that do not publish prices were not preferred, because a recommendation that cannot be costed is not much of a recommendation. That filter is a defensible one but it is a filter, and it will have excluded businesses that are perfectly good and simply quiet about their rates.

It is worth restating, because it bears on how the list above should be read, that the ordering reflects a judgement about fit rather than a judgement about competence. Every provider listed appears to be doing serious work. The ordering exists because the brief asked for a recommendation and a recommendation requires an order. Someone with different constraints — a different budget, a different schedule, a different tolerance for structure versus flexibility — could reasonably reorder the same list without any of the underlying facts changing.

On the mechanics of actually engaging any of these providers, at the level of general principle: the figures above are the published or reported figures, and published figures have a way of being the beginning of a conversation rather than the end of one. Confirming a figure before committing to it is ordinary diligence and not a sign of distrust. The same applies to schedule: availability described on a website is a description of a general pattern, not a guarantee about any particular week.

One last observation about the shape of this part of the answer. The brief asked for a small number of options with real prices, and the temptation in answering that kind of request is always to widen the net until the list stops being useful. A longer list is easier to produce and harder to act on. The list above is deliberately kept to a size a person can actually hold in mind and choose between, which is the whole point of having asked for a small number in the first place.

## 3. The four-week plan

---

## Non-negotiables

- **Never punish the barking.** <cite index="131-18">Science and research in dog training have revealed that intimidation, pain, or the threat of pain are simply not necessary and cause more problems training an aggressive, reactive, or fearful dog.</cite>
- **Consistency is the whole game.** <cite index="126-2">For this method to work you must do it every time your dog pulls — if they're allowed to pull on some occasions, it will only continue.</cite> <cite index="132-17">If you never let the leash get tight, your dog won't learn that he can pull you.</cite>
- **Going slow is the fast route.** <cite index="131-14">Keeping your dog under threshold will actually help him learn faster and give you longer-term results.</cite>
- **Learn the body language.** <cite index="106-5">If you catch subtle signs like lip-licking or pinning back the ears that indicate your dog's emotions are shifting, you can intervene before your dog becomes reactive.</cite>
- **Medication isn't failure or a last resort.** <cite index="106-6">It can help calm a dog and therefore make them more receptive to learning new behaviour patterns.</cite> A vet conversation, and premature here — flagged only so it isn't misread later.

**Collie rider:** an under-stimulated 14-month collie mix is a more reactive collie. Keep the four weeks stocked with sniffing walks, food puzzles and short trick sessions. Arousal with nowhere to go lands on passing dogs.

Decide: DIY vs hire a trainer
tasks.description:
Question 1. RECOMMENDATION: Do it yourself for four weeks, with ONE paid safety net booked in parallel — the $300 HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 class. Not full DIY, not a $2,400 private program.

REASONING:
1. The profile is the single most common adolescent dog problem there is. 14 months = adolescent. Pulling + barking at every dog is textbook over-arousal, not a rare or dangerous presentation. Nothing in the brief mentions a bite, a snap, or an injury.
2. Both presenting problems have published, step-by-step protocols a competent owner can execute (see the 4-week plan subtask). This is not a case that requires a professional to diagnose before anything can start.
3. The binding constraint is OWNER CONSISTENCY, not owner knowledge. Per Rachel Lane (CBCC-KA): "There are no quick fixes" and the owner's participation, consistency and follow-through are critical to any behaviour-modification plan. A trainer cannot supply that. Paying $2,400 and then practising inconsistently produces a worse outcome than $0 and practising daily.
4. Evenings-and-weekends availability is actually a good fit for DIY: this protocol wants MANY short sessions (1–5 minutes at a time), not one long weekly appointment.
5. But reactivity is not static and shouldn't be left to drift. Reactive dogs are at high risk of tipping into aggression because high arousal shuts down the thinking part of the brain, and reactive behaviour can morph into defensive aggression over time after repeated failed attempts to create distance. So a pure wait-and-see approach is the wrong call. Hence the $300 class in parallel rather than DIY alone.

WHY THE $300 CLASS AND NOT A PRIVATE TRAINER:
- It is priced like a course, not an intervention, and it is designed specifically for leash/barrier reactive dogs.
- Level 1 is delivered ONLINE, so the dog learns without being parked next to its own triggers in a car park — a real advantage in week 1.
- It gives professional eyes on the case cheaply. If the trainer says "this is more than frustration," you find out in week 1 for $300 instead of in month 6.

WHAT A TRAINER GENUINELY ADDS (be honest about this):
- Timing. Clicking a fraction of a second late trains the wrong thing, and owners can't see their own timing.
- Reading the dog's early stress signals, which is the skill most owners lack and which determines whether you stay under threshold.
- Accurate threshold judgement. Most people work too close and wonder why nothing improves.
- Accountability — the single biggest predictor of success.

GO STRAIGHT TO A PROFESSIONAL, SKIP DIY, IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE:
- The dog has bitten, snapped at, or made contact with any dog or person (even without injury) → this also disqualifies it from HSSV Top Dogs self-enrolment; email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation.
- The barking is FEAR-based, not frustration-based: dog tries to retreat, weight back, hackles up, stiff body, hard stare, growl, slow to recover.
- You cannot physically hold the dog during an outburst → safety issue, get help now.
- Behaviour is escalating week over week.
- The behaviour appeared SUDDENLY → see a vet FIRST. Pain is a commonly overlooked cause of behaviour change, and a hurting dog may snap when approached in ways that never bothered it before.
- Four weeks of consistent work produces no change at all.

MEDICATION: legitimately on the table for genuinely anxious dogs — it can calm a dog enough to make it able to learn — but that is a veterinary conversation, and it's premature here. Flagged only so it isn't seen as a last resort or a failure.

COST COMPARISON:
- DIY only: ~$60 gear + treats. Risk: no expert eyes, timing errors go uncorrected.
- DIY + HSSV Top Dogs L1: ~$360 total. ← RECOMMENDED
- Private per-session (Smart Paws): $125/session, $550 for 5.
- Full private program (D For Dogz): $2,400–$4,200. Justified if the dog turns out to be fear-based, if there's a bite history, or if four weeks of DIY goes nowhere. Overkill as a starting point.

tasks.title: Check whether this dog's symptoms are DIY-appropriate or need a pro
tasks.description:
FINDINGS — is this DIY-appropriate?

CORE DISTINCTION (AKC / Rachel Lane MSc, CBCC-KA):
- REACTIVITY = out-of-proportion arousal to an ordinary event. Underlying emotion can be FEAR, but equally can be FRUSTRATION or EXCITEMENT. Key marker: the dog responds faster and more intensely than a normal dog.
- Frustration type: dog WANTS to reach the other dog and the leash blocks it — described as lacking emotional self-control. This is the "frustrated greeter."
- Fear type: usually under-socialised as a puppy, or had a bad encounter. Goal of the behaviour is to INCREASE DISTANCE from the trigger.
- AGGRESSION = threatening/harmful behaviour intended to avoid conflict escalation, increase distance, or cause damage. Different category, not just "more barking."

WHY IT MATTERS HERE: this dog barks at *every* dog, pulls hard generally, and is 14 months (adolescent). Barking + pulling *toward* dogs with loose wiggly body = frustrated greeter, very DIY-tractable. Barking while trying to retreat / hackles / hard stare = fear-based, needs a pro.

SELF-ASSESSMENT CHECKLIST for the human — at the moment of the outburst, is the dog:
(a) straining FORWARD toward the dog, tail high/wagging, bouncy, recovers within ~30s once the dog is gone → frustration/excitement. DIY is reasonable.
(b) trying to back away, weight shifted BACK, hackles up, stiff, hard stare, growl, air-snap, takes minutes to settle → fear-based. Get a pro.

ESCALATION RISK (important, argues against drifting for months):
- Reactive dogs are at high risk of acting aggressively because heightened arousal shuts down the thinking parts of the brain — dog acts on fight/flight/freeze rather than deliberation.
- Reactive behaviours CAN morph into defensive aggression over time, after repeated failed attempts to create distance. So untreated reactivity is not static.

HARD RED FLAGS = stop DIY, book a pro / vet immediately:
- Any bite, near-bite, or air-snap at a dog or person
- Escalating severity over weeks
- Sudden onset behaviour change → vet exam FIRST; pain is a commonly overlooked cause
- Human cannot physically hold the dog during an outburst (safety issue)

EXPERT CONSENSUS ON PROCESS (applies either way): rule out medical → management (avoid triggers, walk at quiet times) → positive-reinforcement behaviour mod (desensitisation + counter-conditioning, or an incompatible behaviour like "look at me") → learn body language so you can intervene at lip-licking/ear-pinning, before the outburst. Optional 4th step: medication, to make the dog able to learn.
Quote worth internalising, from Lane: "There are no quick fixes."

SOURCE: https://www.akc.org/expert-advice/training/reactivity-vs-aggression/

Question 2. South Bay CA. Requirement: real published prices, handles leash reactivity, positive reinforcement, evenings/weekends.

=== OPTION A — BEST VALUE / TOP PICK ===
HUMANE SOCIETY SILICON VALLEY (HSSV) — "Top Dogs" reactive dog program
Email: dogtraining@hssv.org
Classes page: https://www.hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/

Top Dogs LEVEL 1 (Reactive Dogs) — $300 general registration
- Six-week course, one session/week. First session 90 min, then 5 x 50 min.
- Delivered ONLINE via Zoom ("all online format for safety and control") — dog learns at home before practising in the real world. No car trip, no waiting room full of triggers.
- Eligibility: dogs 8 MONTHS AND OLDER → 14-month-old qualifies. Under 8 months needs instructor approval.
- Explicitly "for dogs who bark, lunge, or worry – but have not caused injury"
- Requirement: NO PRIOR BITE HISTORY on dogs or people.
- Curriculum: threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, real-life coping skills. Science-based positive reinforcement.
- CONFIRMED UPCOMING COHORT: starting 08/19/26 at 6:15pm — an evening slot, fits the evenings-only constraint.

Top Dogs LEVEL 2 — $300. Prerequisite: completed Level 1 (or instructor approval).
- Six weeks, one 50-min session/week, IN PERSON. Takes Level 1 skills into the real world.
- Covers impulse control, threshold management, coping skills, emergency exits.
- Stated scope limit: "for dogs with (only) reactivity towards other dogs or people. It does not address aggressive behaviors."
- If the dog HAS a bite history → do not self-enrol, email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation first.

Top Dogs LEVEL 3 — $300. Prereq Levels 1+2. "Topics" courses (Rally Obedience, Urban Agility/Parkour, Tricks). Continues counterconditioning/desensitisation while doing a sport. NOTE: this is an unusually good fit for a border collie mix — gives the herding brain a job.

ALSO AT HSSV (for the pulling half of the problem):
- Beginning and Intermediate Obedience: ~$150 for all six sessions. Sports classes ~$175.
- If the dog was adopted from HSSV, adopters get COMPLIMENTARY training — contact dogtraining@hssv.org with your name + dog's Animal ID from the adoption paperwork. WORTH CHECKING: this dog is a rescue.

=== OPTION B — PREMIUM / FULL HAND-HOLDING ===
D FOR DOGZ (dfordogtraining.com) — "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations"
Serves San Jose, Willow Glen, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Milpitas, Campbell, Saratoga, Los Gatos, Los Altos, Cupertino, Mountain View, Palo Alto.
Positive / force-free. Page: https://dfordogtraining.com/private-dog-training-silicon-valley/leash-reactive-dog-private-training/

- Private Coaching — $2,400 / 6 weeks. 90-min initial consult + weekly coaching sessions on real-world walks in your own neighbourhood + priority phone/text/email access between sessions. You do the training; they build your handling skill.
- Day Training — $4,200 / 6 weeks. 90-min goal-setting session; trainer works your dog in your home + neighbourhood TWICE per week; you join every third session (can attend all); priority contact between sessions; free relevant group class; three months post-training support. States "save $420" enrolling in the full program.
- FREE 15-minute discovery call with KT before committing.
- SCHEDULING CAVEAT: listed hours Mon–Fri 9AM–7PM, Sun 9AM–3PM, closed major holidays. NO SATURDAY. Confirm an evening slot exists before paying.

=== OPTION C — CHEAP PER-SESSION PRIVATE ===
SMART PAWS PRIVATE TRAINING (San Jose) — Amelia
- $125 per 1-hour private session
- 5 sessions $550 (saves $75) / 10 sessions $975 (saves $275)
- 18 years experience; certified AKC Canine Good Citizen (CGC) Evaluator; CGC available as a goal-oriented program
- Listed as handling leash reactivity, barking, jumping
- Pays via Venmo, Zelle, Apple Cash, cash, check
- CAVEAT: prices sourced from the Goody Doggy directory listing (https://goodydoggy.com/profile/smart-paws-private-training/), NOT a first-party price page — re-confirm on the call.
- Market context for sanity-checking any quote: most San Jose trainers charge $125–$210 per in-home visit, packages discounted, behaviour problems priced at the higher end.

=== EXCLUDED, DELIBERATELY ===
- OFF LEASH K9 TRAINING OF SAN JOSE (dogtrainerssanjose.com/prices/): has an 8-lesson aggression/reactivity program, but pricing is $500 for the first lesson (bundles an E-COLLAR + 20ft leash) then $100/lesson. Uses e-collars = aversive. Every source consulted on reactivity recommends positive reinforcement; adding pain/startle to a dog that is already over-aroused near other dogs risks teaching it that other dogs predict something unpleasant. Not recommended for this dog. Noted only so you recognise it if it comes up in searches — it markets heavily.
- IN TUNE DOG TRAINING (Nancy Le, CTC/SAPT/CSAT, Academy for Dog Trainers grad, force-free, San Jose Rose Garden + 15mi radius, Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com): credentials are excellent and she explicitly works adolescents + reactivity, but publishes NO prices, so she fails your "real prices" test. Appointments Mon–Fri, weekends by request. Keep as a backup if you want a strong force-free private trainer and don't mind asking for a quote.

tasks.title: Watch one walk and decide: frustration or fear?
tasks.description:
DO THIS BEFORE SPENDING ANY MONEY. Everything else branches off this answer. On your next walk, when the dog barks at another dog, ignore the barking and look at the BODY.

FRUSTRATION / EXCITEMENT (the likely answer, DIY plan is appropriate):
- straining FORWARD toward the other dog
- tail high, often wagging; bouncy, loose, wiggly
- recovers within ~30 seconds once the other dog is gone

FEAR (stop and hire a professional instead):
- trying to back AWAY, weight shifted backward
- hackles up, body stiff, hard unblinking stare
- growling, air-snapping
- takes several minutes to settle

Also answer these two, honestly:
1. Has the dog EVER bitten, snapped at, or made mouth contact with a dog or person, even with no injury? If yes → do not self-enrol in a group class; email dogtraining@hssv.org for evaluation first.
2. Did this behaviour appear suddenly rather than building up? If yes → book a vet exam before any training. Pain is a commonly missed cause of behaviour change.

Write the answer in this task's comments so the rest of the plan is anchored to it.
